1. Vide this judgment, I shall decide a suit for recovery of Rs.1,31,448/.
BRIEF FACTS OF THE PLAINT:
2. The brief facts of the plaint which are necessary for adjudication of the present suit are that:

a) The plaintiff is the proprietor of Balaji Sales Corporation having its office at Hauz Qazi, Delhi and is engaged in the business of trading, distribution and marketing of welding accessories, safety equipment, electrodes of esab, rubber hose pipe and sheets.
b) The defendant No.1 is a Private Limited company registered under The Companies Act, 1956 and the defendants No.2 to 4 are its Directors, responsible for its day to day routine work and that defendants No.2 to 4 on behalf of defendant No.1 telephonically placed orders from their registered office at Badarpur, Delhi110 044 and had been purchasing different sorts of material from the plaintiff from time to time.
c) The defendants placed orders for different sort of goods from time to time which were duly supplied to them from 31.10.2014 to 25.11.2014 through tax invoices and the same were duly received by the defendants at their office. That as per the statement of accounts maintained by the plaintiff qua defendant No.1 in its due course of business, the last transaction was on 13.04.2015 and the relevant entry in the ledger account was made thereof. Thereafter, defendants neither placed any Sanjeev Jain vs Food And Biotech Engineers (India) Pvt ... on 15 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/172803579/
2 orders nor made any payment CS No.2911/2016 Pg 3 of 23 Sanjeev Jain v. Food and Biotech Engineers (India) Pvt. Ltd. towards the outstanding payment of Rs.1,31,448/ which includes Rs.1,03,502/ towards the principal amount and Rs.27,946/ towards interest at the rate of 18% for per annum. 
d) That as per the custom and usage of business as well as agreed terms, the defendants are liable to pay interest at the rate of 36% per annum on the outstanding amount from the date of last transaction i.e. 13.04.2015 but despite repeated reminders and requests, the defendants have neither paid the principal amount nor any interest. 
e) On 16.01.2016, plaintiff even sent a legal notice to the defendants through its Advocate demanding the outstanding payment within 15 days from the receipt of the said notice, however, the defendants have failed to pay the same despite service of legal notice. 
3. Hence, the present suit for recovery of Rs.1,31,448/ along with pendentelite and future interest at the rate of 18% per annum. WRITTEN STATEMENT:

It has further been submitted that since, the defendant No.1 procures materials in bulk, by the time defendant No.1 came to know through its officials that the plaintiff has supplied inferior quality material, a lot of material was already consumed. The officials of defendant No.1 called the plaintiff and informed about the same and after discussion with the plaintiff in detail about the total loss incurred by the defendant, said debit note was issued which plaintiff has acknowledged by its email dated 27.02.2015.

It has thereafter been denied that the defendants are liable to pay the outstanding payment or interest at the rate of 36% per annum. The receipt of legal notice dated 16.01.2016 has also been denied. Accordingly, it has been prayed that the suit of the plaintiff is liable to be dismissed.

a) Ex.DW1/1 Board resolution dated 20.03.2023.
b) Ex.DW1/2 was deexhibited and marked as MarkDX1 being photocopy of Debit/Credit Note.
c) Ex.DW1/3 was deexhibited and marked as MarkA being photocopy of letter dated 27.02.2015.

It was argued on behalf of the plaintiff that DW1 has admitted the fact that the total purchases amounting to Rs.5,99,276/ as shown in the ledger account maintained by the plaintiff were made by defendant No.1 from the plaintiff. It has also been admitted that the CForm amounting to Rs.5,99,276/ (Ex.PW1/3) was also issued by the CS No.2911/2016 Pg 8 of 23 Sanjeev Jain v. Food and Biotech Engineers (India) Pvt. Ltd. defendant No.1. Accordingly, it was argued that since the defendants have failed to place on record any material to show the return of goods or that the same were of inferior quality, the plaintiff is entitled to a decree in his favour. 
12. Per contra, it was argued on behalf of the defendants that there was no dispute with respect to the fact of purchases as made by the defendant No.1 from the plaintiff. However, some of the goods as supplied by the plaintiff were of inferior quality owing to which debit note (MarkDX1) was issued which has been admitted by the PW1 qua which a reply was also issued by the plaintiff (Mark A). Further, it was argued that the fact that inferior quality goods were supplied to the defendants is clear from the email exchange between the parties which contains several test reports from both the sides. The ld. Counsel for the defendants also argued on the misjoinder of defendants No.2 to 4 as parties in the present suit as they were only Directors of defendant No.1. 
Reliance was placed upon the judgments of the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi titled Sanuj Bathla v.
Manu Maheshwari & Anr. dated 12.04.2021 and Tristar Consultants v.
CS No.2911/2016 Pg 9 of 23 Sanjeev Jain v. Food and Biotech Engineers (India) Pvt. Ltd. Vcustomer Services India Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. AIR 2007 Del 157 in support of the same. 
13. I have heard the arguments and perused the record. Before proceeding further with findings upon the issues, it is relevant to mention that it is the case of the plaintiff that defendants made a total purchase of Rs.5,99,276/ from the plaintiff out of which part payments were duly made and only the payment of Rs.1,03,502/ remained to be paid by the defendants for which the present suit has been filed. The defendants have also admitted to the said facts qua purchase and part payments,
however, it is their case that in view of receipt of damaged/inferior quality goods, the defendants had raised a debit note for the remaining sum of Rs.1,03,502/ and thus, have no liability to pay the same to the plaintiff.

5 14. Accordingly, my issuewise findings as follows:
ISSUE NO.1:
Whether the plaintiff is entitled to the recovery of Rs.1,31,448/? OPP.
15. The said amount includes principal sum of Rs.1,03,502/ and Rs.27,946/ as presuit interest @ 18% per annum. For the sake of CS No.2911/2016 Pg 10 of 23 Sanjeev Jain v. Food and Biotech Engineers (India) Pvt. Ltd. clarity, the Court is restricting itself to the principal amount only while giving its findings upon the present issue and the interest part shall be dealt alongwith issue No.2.
16. The onus to prove the said issue was upon the plaintiff. The plaintiff to discharge this onus has examined its AR/ PW1 Sh. Suresh Kumar who deposed on the lines of the plaint. PW1 relied upon the original invoices (Ex.PW1/1), copy of bilties (Ex.PW1/2), copy of CForm (Ex.PW1/3) and account statement (Ex.PW1/4) in support of his case. The plaintiff also filed the certificate under Section 65B Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (Ex.PW1/5) in support of the invoices and statement of accounts. No material contradictions were brought forth during the crossexamination of the said witness qua the said documents. The only pertinent fact that came forth in the cross examination of the said witness was that he had never personally dealt with or was involved in any transactions that took place between the plaintiff and defendants. However, it also came on record that he managed the recovery of dues of the plaintiff's firm M/s. Balaji Traders from its clients and since the present suit relates to recovery of said dues only, it cannot be said that PW1 had no personal knowledge of CS No.2911/2016 Pg 11 of 23 Sanjeev Jain v. Food and Biotech Engineers (India) Pvt.
Ltd. the facts of the present case which would make his testimony immaterial. What is also imperative to note here is that the case of the plaintiff was admitted by DW1 wherein, during his crossexamination, DW1 admitted that the transactions from points A to A1 as marked in the statement of account as relied upon by the plaintiff (Ex.PW1/4) amounting to Rs.5,99,276/ were made by the defendant No.1 from the plaintiff. DW1 further admitted that the CForm, Ex.PW1/3 amounting to Rs.5,99,276/ was issued by defendant No.1. In the given circumstances, the Court is satisfied that the plaintiff has been able to discharge its initial burden to prove recovery in its favour and now the onus shifts upon the defendants to prove that they were not entitled to make any payment to the plaintiff. 
17. The defendants to discharge this onus have examined their AR/DW1 Sh. Rajveer Singh who has deposed on the lines of the written statement. DW1 has relied upon MarkDX1 (photocopy of debit note dated 13.02.2015 for a sum of Rs.1,03,502/) and MarkA (reply dated 27.02.2015) in support of its case that inferior quality goods were supplied to the defendants for which defendants were not bound to make any payment and accordingly, issued the said debit note which CS No.2911/2016 Pg 12 of 23 Sanjeev Jain v. Food and Biotech Engineers (India) Pvt. Ltd. was duly acknowledged by the plaintiff vide the said reply. It is the case of the defendants that they had ordered frill wire of SS 304 quality but the plaintiff malafidely supplied them with frill wire of SS 202 quality, in view of which the debit note for return of the said goods was issued. The defendants have further argued that PW 1, in his crossexamination has admitted to having no knowledge about the transactions between the parties and also that indeed, a debit note was received by the plaintiff from defendant No.1 but Sanjeev Jain vs Food And Biotech Engineers (India) Pvt ... on 15 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/172803579/
6 he did not know whether MarkDX1 was the said note. Further, it is argued that debit note in question was issued electronically on the email id of the plaintiff and since PW1 has admitted that he neither has access to nor has any information about the email address of the plaintiff and since the documents as relied upon by the plaintiff nowhere mention any debit note, the natural corollary to the same is that the debit note MarkDX1 is the same debit note. Accordingly, it is argued that the plaintiff has admitted to receiving the debit note and thus, the defendants are not liable to make any payment to the plaintiff. 
18. The Court is of the view that merely filing a debit note would not absolve the defendants of its liability towards the plaintiff and its CS No.2911/2016 Pg 13 of 23 Sanjeev Jain v. Food and Biotech Engineers (India) Pvt. Ltd. evidentiary value also has to be seen. At the foremost, no explanation has been brought forth as to why originals of the said two documents i.e. MarkA and MarkDX1 have not been filed on record. Secondly, defendants have raised certain pleas with regard to two types of frill wires and that an inferior quality frill wire was supplied to them as opposed to the superior quality one that they ordered but no evidence has been brought forth as to the description of wires ordered and the ones delivered. Now, since the invoices as relied upon by the plaintiff do not contain any such details of the description of wires ordered, it was upon the defendants to lead evidence to this effect which has not been done. Further, although the ld. Counsel for the defendants relied upon certain quality reports as exchanged between the parties through email qua the inferior quality of the goods, but such documents were never formally brought on record, they were never relied upon by the defendants in their evidence nor any separate witnesses were examined to prove them. In such a case, the said documents cannot be looked into by this Court and the Court has no documents to decide whether the goods that were delivered to the defendants were of inferior quality. 
CS No.2911/2016 Pg 14 of 23 Sanjeev Jain v. Food and Biotech Engineers (India) Pvt. Ltd. 
19 . Now, although, there is no express admission by the PW1 with regard to the MarkDX1 but even if for arguments sake, it is presumed that the debit note was duly generated and that reply was also issued by the plaintiff to the same, it still does not explain as to why no material was brought on record on behalf of the defendants to show as to what steps were taken after receipt of the said reply as the same stated "...So, we request you that kindly release our full payment OR return the material so that we return it to the manufacturer and claim our loss." The defendants have failed to bring on record any material to show whether the said goods were returned to the plaintiff or what efforts were made to do the same. This becomes especially relevant as it is the defendants' own averments in the written statement as well evidence affidavit that, "...The defendant No.1 procures materials in bulk and by the time the officials of the defendant No.1 came to know that the plaintiff has supplied the inferior quality material, a lot of the material has already been consumed. The officials of defendant No.1 called the plaintiff and informed about the said discrepancy and only after discussion with the plaintiff in detail about the total loss had issued the said debit note...". Since defendants themselves admit that a lot of the material had CS No.2911/2016 Pg 15 of 23 Sanjeev Jain v. Food and Biotech Engineers (India) Pvt. Ltd. already been consumed, the fact that the same were sought to be returned goes out of the question. If the defendants had any grievance about the quality of goods, especially if they had already been consumed, the only remedy that they had was to file a separate suit for recovery of compensation or damages which has not been done. The Sanjeev Jain vs Food And Biotech Engineers (India) Pvt ... on 15 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/172803579/
7 defendants could also have a filed a counterclaim along with their written statement, which again has not been done. Moreover, admittedly, the goods were supplied in October and November, 2014 but the debit note, if presumed to be genuine, is dated 13.02.2015. In such a case, when the return of goods was sought after around three months, it was all the more incumbent upon the defendants to take effective steps if they had any grievance towards the quality of the goods received and wanted to return the same but nothing has been brought on record to show the same. In the given circumstances, in the absence of any material to show that inferior quality goods were supplied coupled with the admission that some of the alleged inferior quality goods were also consumed, the Court is of the view that the defendants have failed to discharge their onus. Therefore, they cannot avoid payment of the goods which they CS No.2911/2016 Pg 16 of 23 Sanjeev Jain v. Food and Biotech Engineers (India) Pvt. Ltd. have admittedly duly received. 
20. Accordingly, issue No.1 is decided in favour of the plaintiff and against the defendants. 
ISSUE NO.2:
Whether the plaintiff is entitled to any pendentelite and future interest at the rate of 18% per annum on the suit amount, if yes, at what rate, for which period? OPP. 
21. In view of the fact that the issue No.1 has been decided in favour of the plaintiff, it naturally flows that the defendants were liable to make payment to the plaintiff which they have failed to do and thus, are liable to pay interest on such late payment. Although, the invoices as relied upon by the plaintiff do mention that interest @ 18% will be charged if payment is not made within the stipulated time period but no evidence has been brought forth as to the rate of interest or within what period, the said payment was to be made. It is settled law that the Court is not bound by the rate of interest as claimed by the plaintiff even if contractual. The Court should be alive to the change of rate of interest regime and should refrain from awarding excessively high and unreasonable rates of interest (reference can be made to the judgment of Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in the case of M/s. Sangat CS No.2911/2016 Pg 17 of 23 Sanjeev Jain v. Food and Biotech Engineers (India) Pvt. Ltd. Printers Pvt. Ltd. v. M/s. Wimpy International Ltd. RFA No.657/2003) . 
In the given circumstances, since the interest @ 18% per annum seems unreasonable, the Court deems it fit to exercise its discretion under Section 34 of CPC and award interest @ 7% per annum. 
22. Now coming to the period from which the said interest is to be payable. The plaint is silent as to the exact date from which presuit interest has been calculated and merely mentions that the same has been calculated from its due date. In the given circumstances, the Court deems it fit to award interest from the date of the last payment i.e. 13.04.2015 till its actual realization. 
23. Accordingly, issue No.2 is decided in favor of the plaintiff. 
ISSUE NO.3:
Whether the suit is bad for nonjoinder of necessary parties? OPD.

8 24. It is the case of the defendants that the transaction in question took place between the plaintiff and defendant No.1 company and the defendants No.2 to 4, being merely Directors of the latter,
can not be individually impleaded in the present suit as parties. Now, although averments to this effect have been made in the written statement, but CS No.2911/2016 Pg 18 of 23 Sanjeev Jain v.
Food and Biotech Engineers (India) Pvt. Ltd. no evidence has been led qua the same. The evidence by way of affidavit of DW1, Ex.DW1/A is completely silent upon the same and even no questions or suggestions were put to PW1 in this regard. However, during final arguments, certain citations in support of the said averment were relied upon by the defendants and since, the factum of impleadment of Directors of a company is a legal question, the Court is of the opinion that the same can be decided on the basis of available record. 
25. It is settled law that a company, being a juristic person, can only act through its Directors, who are its agents, representatives, trustees. Such agents act for and on behalf of the company, on the basis of and in line with the authority given to them by the Company. But the Directors owe no fiduciary or contractual duty to the third parties who deal with the company unless they act in a malafide manner for their own personal gains. Reference in this regard can be made to the judgment of the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in the case of Tristar Consultants v. Customer Services India Pvt.
Ltd. & Anr. 139 (2007) DLT 688 wherein the following observations were made:
CS No.2911/2016 Pg 19 of 23 Sanjeev Jain v. Food and Biotech Engineers (India) Pvt. Ltd.
"19. It is settled law that a company is a juristic person . Therefore, a company has to act through a living human being. Collectively, decisions on behalf of the company,
are taken by the board of Directors of a company. An individual director has no power to act on behalf of a company of which he is a director, unless there is a specific resolution of the board of Directors of the company giving specific power to him/her, or, where the articles of company confer such an power.
20. Directors of companies have been described as agents, trustees or representatives of the company because of the fact visavis the company they act in a fiduciary capacity. They perform acts and duties for the benefit of the company. Thus,
Directors are agents of the company to the extent they have been authorized to perform certain acts on behalf of the company. 
21. But Directors of a company owe no fiduciary or contractual duties or any duty of care to third parties who deal with the company. 
22. This distinction has been ignored by learned Counsel for the petitioner. 
23. Directors of a company are referred to as agents of the company in the context of their fiduciary duty to the company and therefore if they derive any personal benefit while purporting to act on behalf of the company, they will be liable to the company and its shareholders. But the Directors cannot be CS No.2911/2016 Pg 20 of 23 Sanjeev Jain v. Food and Biotech Engineers (India) Pvt. Ltd. treated as acting as Sanjeev Jain vs Food And Biotech Engineers (India) Pvt ... on 15 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/172803579/ 
9 agents of the company, in the conventional sense of an agent, visavis third parties. 
... 
28. To interpret the law as is sought to be projected by the petitioner would mean negation of the concept of a company being limited by its liability as per the memorandum and articles of association of the company. Other than where Directors have made themselves personally liable i.e. by way of guarantee, indemnity etc.
liabilities of Directors of a company, under common law, are confined to cases of malfiescence and misfiescence i.e. where they have been guilty of tort towards those to whom they owe a duty of care i.e. discharge fiduciary obligations. Additionally, qua third parties, where Directors have committed tort. To the third party, they may be personally liable. 
29. For example by making false representations about a company, a director induces a third party to advance a loan to the company. On proof of fraudulent misrepresentation, a director may be personally liable to the third party. 
30. But this liability would not flow from a contract but would flow in an action at tort. The tort being of misrepresentation of inducement and causing injury to the third party having induced the third party to part with money." 
CS No.2911/2016 Pg 21 of 23 Sanjeev Jain v. Food and Biotech Engineers (India) Pvt.
Ltd.
26. Thus, what transpires is that to make the Directors of a company liable for its debts, it has to be proved that they personally indemnified or gave guarantee to be responsible for the debts of the company and that they were guilty of misconduct in the company's affairs. In the case at hand, no such averments have been made either in the plaint or evidence affidavit, Ex.PW1/A. It has merely been mentioned that defendants No. 2 to 4 were responsible for running the daytoday affairs of defendant No.1 company. In the given circumstances, no case has been made out as to why the corporate veil should be lifted and the Directors be made personally liable for the debts of the company. 
27. However, the mere impleadment of the Directors in a suit for recovery of dues from the company would not entail dismissal of the suit when the company has also been made a party. Such misjoinder is curable and would not make the suit bad. 
28. In view of the above findings, issue No.3 is decided.
